post:
Before a smart meter's 15-minute data can be billed, someone has to deal with the gaps, spikes, stuck values, duplicates and clocks that missed the daylight-saving switch. The open question is how long a gap can get before the estimate is no longer fair to bill.

I built an open-source VEE tool (validation, estimation, editing) and measured it on 34 months of a real household's open data, with 416 simulated faults injected into the meter file. Eight rules flag the faults; linear interpolation, a similar-day profile or a temperature regression fills them; every edit keeps its original value, method, rule and time in an audit trail.

Measured:
- Without register reads, an estimated gap of up to 8 h stays under 1 % of the month's kWh (p90, my own yardstick); at 1 day one gap in ten exceeds it, at 7 days 8 %.
- With daily register reads, monthly energy after repair was at most 0.77 % off; as received, up to 384 %.
- 12 of 12 clock shifts were found and undone exactly.

Not verified: one household and simulated faults, no utility meter-data system. And for 15-minute tariffs no method was good enough past an hour or two.

Where do you draw the line between estimating and asking for a re-read?

Code: https://github.com/VB-Builds/interval-data-vee
